editions.title: Nvidia's Jensen Huang faces board probe over spy reports
editions.notification: Nvidia's CEO is under an independent probe over reported China spy links. Here's what we know so far.
editions.intro:
The dominant story is the crisis at Nvidia. Chief executive Jensen Huang has apologised in an internal memo for an affair, after The New York Times reported that US agencies were examining Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive, over suspected links to China's Ministry of State Security. Nvidia's board has opened an independent investigation, supported by outside counsel, and says it sees no sign that national security or company secrets were compromised. Huang remains CEO. Three Republican House committee chairs have asked for a briefing by 11 November, and Singapore has opened its own probe into Megaspeed. The Chinese government and embassy deny the espionage allegations, and no one has been charged. The suspected operation has not been independently confirmed.

The episode matters well beyond gossip. Nvidia sits at the centre of AI chip supply, and Megaspeed reportedly bought billions of dollars of its chips, while the US Commerce Department has accused the firm of smuggling $2 billion of advanced chips to China. Nvidia shares fell more than 9% in a single session, their steepest daily drop since January 2025, amid a wider chip sell-off that also hit Asian markets. Analysts such as Jeffrey Sonnenfeld put Huang's chances of surviving the probe at roughly even.

Elsewhere, the AI-infrastructure backlash is gathering pace. A new analysis found about 90% of public comments at local government meetings opposed data centres, a Michigan Democrat who campaigned against them won a seat in Congress, and a Texas town-level ban passed with about 77% support. Samsung and SK hynix together hold 329 trillion won in cash, funding record chip spending and shareholder returns.

top_stories.title: Huang apologises for affair as board opens independent probe
top_stories.summary: Nvidia's CEO admitted an affair in a letter to staff, while the board said it has no reason to believe secrets or national security were compromised. An independent committee will investigate reported intelligence concerns over Alice Huang, whom US officials reportedly linked to Beijing. The suspected operation has not been independently confirmed.

top_stories.title: House chairs call Huang to closed-door briefing
top_stories.summary: Three Republican House committee chairs have arranged a closed-door meeting with Huang over national security concerns tied to Megaspeed. Singapore has opened its own probe, and Nvidia says its customer meetings are routine. The briefing is due by 11 November.

top_stories.title: Analysts weigh whether Huang can survive the probe
top_stories.summary: Yale's Jeffrey Sonnenfeld puts Huang's odds of staying on at about 50-50. The affair raises questions about Nvidia's AI investments and its dealings with Megaspeed, which bought about $2 billion of chips. Investors will watch the investigation's findings closely.

top_stories.title: Nvidia eyes Brightspeed sites for small AI data centres
top_stories.summary: According to The Information, Nvidia has approached Apollo about converting more than 130 telecom properties into small AI inference data centres, offering about 1 gigawatt across 20 US states. The deal is unconfirmed and Brightspeed is reportedly close to bankruptcy. The report followed a steep one-day fall in Nvidia shares.

top_stories.title: Asian stocks rebound after AI share rout
top_stories.summary: Asian markets rallied after a sharp sell-off last week in AI-related shares pushed many regional indices into bear market territory. The source gives few figures, so the size of the recovery is unclear. The bounce suggests some regained confidence.

top_stories.title: Samsung and SK hynix sit on record cash pile
top_stories.summary: The two Korean chipmakers hold 329.3 trillion won in cash, funding a record 84.4 trillion won capex plan at Samsung and shareholder returns of roughly 90 to 110 trillion won. SK hynix is ramping HBM4 output with 14 long-term supply deals. Investors now want cash returns, not just growth.

top_stories.title: Public comments on data centres run 90% negative
top_stories.summary: A private analysis by Prophecy Gov of 10,202 comments across 48 US states found about 90.5% opposed data centres, citing water, power bills and pollution. It is a sample of comments rather than a national poll, but it signals growing local resistance.

rumour_watch.note: Bloomberg's Mark Gurman reports Apple may make Siri agent-like as early as next year, citing sources and a closed-door meeting; credible given his track record, but Apple has not confirmed a timeline.
The Brightspeed-Nvidia conversion plan is reported by The Information with unconfirmed terms and a distressed partner, so treat the scale as provisional.
A student's 491mph drone speed claim is unverified and falls short of the supersonic prize, so it is interesting but not yet credible as a record.
A developer-leaker's claims about macOS 27.3 changes are still in development and may not ship, so cautious reading is warranted.

editions.title: Tech sell-off deepens as Anthropic presses on with IPO and Nvidia faces spy claims
editions.notification: Tech shares slump after the midterms, Tesla winds down Cybertruck, and Anthropic eyes a pre-Thanksgiving IPO.
editions.intro:
Tech markets were rattled this week. The Nasdaq 100 fell 6.4 percent on Thursday, partly recovering on Friday, as rising borrowing costs, heavy AI spending and Democratic midterm wins raised fears of slower data-centre construction. Tesla shares fell 11 percent after Elon Musk said Cybertruck production will wind down around mid-2027, with the Texas plant shifting to the Cybercab robotaxi and Optimus robots. SpaceX dropped 9 percent in the same session, and Musk's fortune reportedly fell by $113bn.

Against that backdrop, Anthropic is reportedly pressing ahead with an IPO before Thanksgiving, seeking $80 to $100 billion at a valuation of $1.25 to $1.75 trillion, below some investors' hopes. OpenAI has reportedly trimmed its funding-round target and raised only about a third of what it sought, though a separate report claims $11bn new funding at a $1.25 trillion valuation. Both are unconfirmed in the material provided.

Nvidia faces its own storm. Three House committee chairs have arranged a closed-door meeting with Jensen Huang over reports that Megaspeed executive Alice Huang may have been recruited by China's intelligence services. Nvidia says its customer contacts are routine, and China has dismissed the claims. Meanwhile, the memory boom continues: DRAM prices are soaring, Samsung's cash pile passed 200 trillion won, and Raspberry Pi and Oppo are feeling the squeeze. Samsung's Taylor, Texas plant may start trial runs in December.

top_stories.title: Tesla to wind down Cybertruck as Musk pivots to robotaxis and robots
top_stories.summary: Musk said on X that Cybertruck production at Texas will end around mid-2027, freeing space for Cybercab and Optimus. Tesla shares fell 11 percent on Thursday, with SpaceX down 9 percent, after Musk-backed Republicans lost the midterms.

top_stories.title: Anthropic reportedly pushes ahead with IPO at a lower valuation
top_stories.summary: The FT reports Anthropic wants to raise $80 to $100 billion before Thanksgiving at $1.25 to $1.75 trillion, below the $2 trillion some hoped for. The move comes amid a broad tech sell-off, and OpenAI has reportedly trimmed its own funding target.

top_stories.title: Congress calls Jensen Huang over reported Chinese spy link
top_stories.summary: House chairs have asked Nvidia's chief to explain links to Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who was reportedly watched by US agencies over China ties. Neither has been charged, and Nvidia says it would be warned if the government saw a threat.

top_stories.title: Samsung's Texas foundry may begin trial runs in December
top_stories.summary: Samsung's Taylor plant could start trial operations in mid-to-late December, with mass production next year. The site is expected to make Tesla's AI6 chips under a $16.5 billion deal, though the project is about two years late.

top_stories.title: No end in sight for the GPU and memory squeeze
top_stories.summary: DRAM prices are reportedly up about 400 percent since 2024, and Nvidia's RTX 5090 sells well above its launch price. Major memory makers are shifting capacity to AI memory and expect tight supply through 2027 and 2028.

top_stories.title: Samsung's cash pile passes 200 trillion won
top_stories.summary: Samsung reported 214.8 trillion won in cash at the end of Q3 and plans record capital spending of 84.4 trillion won. It can return 90 to 110 trillion won to shareholders this year.

top_stories.title: METR says Anthropic may have crossed its AI acceleration warning line
top_stories.summary: METR's audit suggests Anthropic's rate of model improvement has roughly doubled, with much of the speed-up attributed to AI helping its own research. METR still rates acute catastrophic risk as low, but says the public risk report understated the acceleration.

rumour_watch.note: An FT-relayed claim of a romantic link between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang; Nvidia denies it and the story notes inconsistencies, so treat as unverified.
Single-source FT report citing investors; the valuation range and timing are plausible given reported市场 conditions but not confirmed by Anthropic.
Industry sources on Samsung's Taylor timeline are credible given the company has already installed equipment, though the December date is not official.
Speculation about an earlier GTA VI PC release driven by AI clones is weakly sourced and lacks any Rockstar statement.

editions.title: Tech sell-off deepens as Anthropic eyes $1.5tn IPO
editions.notification: AI stocks slump, Anthropic reportedly eyes a $1.5tn IPO, and Tesla winds down the Cybertruck. Here's the morning brief.
editions.intro:
A sharp tech-led sell-off dominated the period, with the Nasdaq Composite falling 5.5% at one point before recovering 1.1% on Friday. Investors pointed to doubts about returns on AI spending and to the US midterm results, where Democrats' gains raised fears of slower AI development. Asian markets were hit hard, with South Korea's Kospi down 6% and SK Hynix dropping more than 10%, while the FTSE 100 slipped after the Bank of England raised rates.

Against that backdrop, the AI giants are still pressing ahead. The Financial Times reports that Anthropic intends to go ahead with an IPO targeting a valuation of about $1.5tn, with a listing before Thanksgiving. Bloomberg reports OpenAI has been valued at $1.25tn in a fresh round, below the $1.4tn it had hoped for. Political pressure is rising too: Senator Bernie Sanders and several newly elected Democrats are calling for datacentre pauses, and Microsoft is reportedly winding down an Oracle AI-compute rental, a blow to Oracle's shares.

Elsewhere, Tesla confirmed it will end Cybertruck production in Texas around 2027 to make room for Cybercab and Optimus, though Tesla shares rose on Friday after falling 11% the day before. Nvidia reportedly told foreign cloud customers to generate at least half their revenue outside China, a sign of tightening US export pressure. Samsung's mobile staff are protesting over pay as the phone division heads for its first annual loss.

top_stories.title: Anthropic reportedly presses ahead with $1.5tn IPO
top_stories.summary: The Financial Times reports Anthropic plans to go ahead with its IPO despite the sell-off, targeting about $1.5tn and a listing before Thanksgiving. The timing and terms may still change, but a listing would be one of the largest in tech history.

top_stories.title: AI stocks rebound after trillions wiped from markets
top_stories.summary: A tech-led sell-off spread from the US to Asia and Europe, with the Nasdaq partly recovering on Friday. Strong US jobs data and doubts about AI returns and midterm politics drove the volatility.

top_stories.title: OpenAI valued at $1.25tn in smaller-than-hoped round
top_stories.summary: OpenAI's new round values it at $1.25tn, below the $1.4tn it had sought, as tech stocks fell and public opposition to AI grew. Altman says OpenAI will wait for stronger safety claims before listing.

top_stories.title: Democrats push for datacentre pauses after midterms
top_stories.summary: Sanders and newly elected Democrats are calling for national or state pauses on datacentre construction, and voters passed local restrictions. The White House says existing projects will largely continue, but investors are nervous.

top_stories.title: Tesla to wind down Cybertruck production
top_stories.summary: Musk said Cybertruck output in Texas will end around 2027 to free capacity for Cybercab and Optimus. Cybertruck sales fell to about 20,000 in 2025, far below earlier forecasts, and Tesla's shares were volatile.

top_stories.title: Nvidia reportedly requires foreign clouds to earn most revenue outside China
top_stories.summary: The FT reports Nvidia now requires foreign cloud providers to make at least 51% of revenue from outside China, applied to future deals. It follows tighter US export scrutiny and could hit Asian cloud operators.

top_stories.title: Microsoft winds down Oracle AI compute rental
top_stories.summary: Bloomberg reports Microsoft will not renew a 2023 deal to rent AI capacity from Oracle, and is reassessing over $80bn of other cloud contracts. Oracle shares fell about 3% and the company is under credit pressure.

rumour_watch.note: Single-outlet FT report with a 70% rating; the $1.5tn target and Thanksgiving timing are plausible given the reported S-1 filing, but terms may shift.
FT sourcing from people familiar, with a verbal policy, makes this credible at 85%, though Nvidia's public defence suggests the rule is real but not formally published.
Bloomberg with multiple sources and a Microsoft non-denial, plus Oracle's comment, makes the wind-down credible at 80%.
A serious allegation from a single FT feed summary with no response from Nvidia; treat as unconfirmed until further detail emerges.

stocks_to_watch.note: Fell about 3% on reports Microsoft is winding down its AI compute rental, adding to pressure on its cash flow and credit rating.

stocks_to_watch.name: Nvidia
stocks_to_watch.note: Pressured by the sell-off and China-related reports, though its chip software and AI demand remain in focus.

stocks_to_watch.name: Tesla
stocks_to_watch.note: Fell 11% on Thursday, then rose 4.7% on Friday after the Cybertruck wind-down news.

stocks_to_watch.name: SK Hynix
stocks_to_watch.note: Dropped more than 10% in the sell-off, though it is also tied to tight memory demand from OpenAI talks.

stocks_to_watch.name: Samsung Electronics
stocks_to_watch.note: Record profits from memory prices, but staff protests and a likely first mobile loss weigh on sentiment.

stocks_to_watch.name: Amazon
stocks_to_watch.note: Gained on the Anthropic IPO report, given its stake in the AI lab.

Tankers and a fishing boat were seen loitering near Gulf of Oman subsea cables amid Iranian threats to cut them.
Sam Altman met Samsung and SK executives in Korea to discuss memory supply, but no new deal was announced.
Musk says government work will fall below 10% of SpaceX revenue this quarter, with Anthropic a major customer.
The EU has preliminarily found TikTok's ForYou feed harms users' mental health, with fines of up to 6% possible.
A man has sued OpenAI, alleging ChatGPT helped his wife plan a poisoning, the tenth such homicide-related suit.
Rosstat confirmed a cyberattack; hackers claim 23TB of data, but the casualty figures are unverified.

editions.title: Tech shares slump as US midterms revive AI slowdown fears
editions.notification: Nasdaq's worst day in 18 months as Democrats' midterm win sparks data centre curbs fears. Here's what's next.
editions.intro:
Global tech shares suffered their sharpest sell-off in well over a year after Democrats won both houses of Congress in the midterm elections. Investors expect tighter scrutiny of AI data centres, with Democrats having promised a national moratorium on new facilities. The Nasdaq Composite fell about 5.5 per cent on Thursday, its worst day in 18 months, and entered correction territory, wiping out an estimated $2tn to $2.5tn. Nvidia fell 9.2 per cent, and chipmakers including AMD, Micron and Infineon were hit hard across markets.

The contagion spread quickly. Japan's Nikkei dropped below 60,000 points for the first time since May, falling 6.3 per cent at one point, while South Korea's Kospi triggered a circuit breaker after falling more than 8 per cent. Taiwan had its worst week since 2001. The sell-off has also reached credit markets, with SoftBank leading losses in Asian dollar bonds, and Indian equities were among the few gainers in the region. The FTSE 100 was little changed, closing down 0.4 per cent.

The political backdrop is now central to the industry's outlook. Elon Musk spent around $450m backing Republicans and still saw losses, including in Texas, and his companies Tesla and SpaceX fell. OpenAI and Amazon have responded with pledges to drop NDAs with officials and to cover power costs for data centre projects. Meanwhile, the Trump administration has blamed opponents for the fall, so the policy direction for AI infrastructure will be a key thing to watch.

top_stories.title: Global tech stocks plunge as midterms revive AI slowdown fears
top_stories.summary: Tech shares fell across the US, Europe and Asia after Democrats took both houses of Congress, with campaigns focused on slowing data centre growth. Around $2.5tn was wiped from the Nasdaq and the S&P 500 fell 4.4 per cent. Democrats have promised a national data centre moratorium, which investors are pricing in.

top_stories.title: Nasdaq suffers worst day in 18 months, enters correction
top_stories.summary: The Nasdaq Composite fell about 5.5 per cent on Thursday, with Nvidia down 9.2 per cent and the VIX up 61 per cent. Investors are betting that new Democratic governors and lawmakers will curb datacentre expansion. The FTSE 100 closed down 0.4 per cent.

top_stories.title: Asian tech shares sink as Nikkei and Kospi slide
top_stories.summary: The Nikkei 225 dropped below 60,000 for the first time since May, and the Kospi fell under 5,000. The falls followed fears of tighter US regulation of AI data centres after the midterms.

top_stories.title: Musk's midterm spending fails to deliver Republican wins
top_stories.summary: Elon Musk spent almost $450m backing Republicans, more than anyone in a single cycle, but Democrat James Talarico beat Republican Ken Paxton in Texas. The result could bring tougher scrutiny of SpaceX and tech firms, and Tesla and SpaceX shares fell.

top_stories.title: OpenAI pulls back from NDAs for data centre projects
top_stories.summary: OpenAI pledged to drop NDAs with public officials, pay the full cost of its electricity and infrastructure, and publish local job forecasts. The move follows voter opposition to data centre expansion and mirrors an Amazon pledge.

top_stories.summary: The model finds flaws, builds exploits and proposes patches, and is rated 'Critical' under OpenAI's framework. Access is limited to select customers, and all benchmarks come from OpenAI with no independent testing yet.

Macquarie's outgoing chief's view that Australia could benefit from US data centre backlash is an opinion, not a planned project.

editions.title: Midterm shockwaves hit AI and chip stocks; China reportedly blocks SoftBank-ABB deal
editions.notification: Democrats' midterm sweep rattles AI and chip stocks, and China reportedly blocks SoftBank's ABB robotics bid.
editions.intro:
The Democratic sweep of the US midterms dominated the day's tech news. Asian chip stocks slid, with South Korea's Kospi falling as much as 4.67% before a trading halt, and Samsung and SK hynix under pressure. Investors fear a Democrat-led Congress could tighten rules on AI data centres and scrutinise Trump-era AI and crypto trades. US markets recovered on Tuesday, with Nvidia up 2.3%, after the Nasdaq had briefly entered correction territory. Data centres were a clear election issue: an NBC exit poll found almost 80% of respondents opposed them in their neighbourhoods, and local measures restricting construction passed almost everywhere. Musk's record spending of around $450m for Republicans largely failed, and his companies now face likely tougher scrutiny.

Corporate news was mixed. AMD posted a record quarter, with revenue of $13.4bn and data centre making up about 63% of sales, and forecast $17bn next quarter, though its gaming business fell 40%. Apple shares dropped after it warned of thinner margins from higher memory costs. Uber reported strong third-quarter bookings of $59.8bn, but Waymo pulled out of its app in Austin and Atlanta the same day. In Europe and Asia, China reportedly blocked SoftBank's $5.4bn purchase of ABB's robotics unit, an FT report that is not yet confirmed.

Elsewhere, Google will switch off its AI features by default for K-12 student accounts, a move that drew criticism from New York's mayor. Cyber-attacks on European cold storage, including France's blood service, continued, with no group claiming responsibility. Anthropic and OpenAI both announced product and policy updates, including new image watermarking for older Claude models and animated GIF generation in ChatGPT.

top_stories.title: Kospi and chip stocks slump after Democratic midterm sweep
top_stories.summary: South Korean shares fell sharply, with the Kospi down as much as 4.67% and a temporary programme trading halt. Samsung and SK hynix led the drop on fears of tighter US rules on AI data centres.

top_stories.title: Data centres become a midterm issue and a possible regulatory clash
top_stories.summary: Exit polls showed strong opposition to data centres, and local measures restricting them passed in several states. Construction moratoriums and grid-cost rules are likely next, with Goldman Sachs flagging possible delays in Georgia and Texas.

top_stories.title: Local data centre measures largely voted down across the US
top_stories.summary: Of about 40 local measures, only one favoured expansion. Six outright bans passed, and two mayors were recalled over data centre disputes, signalling more scrutiny ahead.

top_stories.title: US tech stocks recover after AI spending selloff
top_stories.summary: The S&P 500 and Nasdaq rose on Tuesday after a brief slide that pushed the Nasdaq into correction. Nvidia gained 2.3% while Apple fell 1.9% on a weaker margin forecast.

top_stories.title: AMD posts record quarter on data centre demand
top_stories.summary: AMD reported record revenue of $13.4bn, with data centre at about 63% of sales. It forecasts $17bn next quarter and over 80% growth in 2027, though gaming revenue fell 40%.

top_stories.title: China reportedly blocks SoftBank's ABB robotics deal
top_stories.summary: The FT reports China's state planner opposed SoftBank's $5.4bn purchase of ABB's robotics arm. The report is unconfirmed, and SoftBank is weighing whether to seek approval again.

top_stories.title: Google ties Search access to AI opt-in for school students
top_stories.summary: Google will turn off Gemini and AI features by default for K-12 accounts, and schools that keep AI disabled will lose Search access. The move reverses an August decision and drew criticism from New York's mayor.

editions.title: Fridge hacks spread across Europe as AMD posts record quarter
editions.notification: Supermarket fridges hacked across Europe, while AMD reports its best quarter ever.
editions.intro:
A suspected cyber-attack is spreading across Europe. Supermarket chains in at least seven countries, including Ahold Delhaize, Ikea, Carrefour Belgium and Colruyt, reported freezer temperatures rising overnight to as high as 50C, and some stores pulled chilled and frozen goods from sale. The EU food commissioner called it a deliberate attempt to disrupt the food supply chain, and experts warned that many refrigeration controllers are reachable online and unpatched. It follows a French attack last month that affected hundreds of supermarkets. The UK's AI minister said a serious cyber breach is "extremely likely", and the NCSC warned that British firms were wilfully blind to threats.

In markets, the story was chipmakers. AMD reported a record $13.4 billion quarter, with data centre revenue of $8.5 billion, and guided to about $17 billion next quarter, while Intel guided to $15-16 billion. Its shares rose about 5% after hours, and analysts see AMD possibly overtaking Intel as the largest x86 chip vendor. AMD's gaming revenue fell 40%, however, as memory shortages driven by AI demand squeeze consumer hardware. Apple also reported a record iPhone quarter of $57.58 billion, up 17%, despite no standard iPhone launch, though it warned of higher memory costs.

Political and market backdrop was volatile. Democrats swept key US midterm races, including Texas, and European and Asian tech shares fell on expectations of tougher scrutiny of Trump-era policies. US tech stocks recovered on Tuesday after the Nasdaq had entered correction territory on Monday. Oracle reportedly dropped a $7 billion Tencent AI deal under US pressure, a single-source report that is worth watching.

top_stories.title: Suspected cyber-attack hits fridges and freezers across Europe
top_stories.summary: Supermarkets in at least seven European countries reported freezer temperatures rising to as high as 50C overnight, with several firms confirming hacks. The EU food commissioner called it a deliberate attempt to disrupt the food supply chain.

top_stories.title: AMD posts its largest and most profitable quarter
top_stories.summary: AMD reported record revenue of $13.4bn, with data centre making up about 63%, and forecast $17bn next quarter. Gaming revenue fell 40% as component shortages hit consumer sales, and AMD expects a down year for consumer markets in 2027.

top_stories.title: Apple posts iPhone sales record without a standard iPhone
top_stories.summary: iPhone revenue rose 17% to $57.58bn, driven by the pricier iPhone 18 Pro models and higher prices on older models. Total revenue rose 12% to $114.5bn, but Apple flagged higher memory costs.

top_stories.title: Democratic win rattles Trump-linked trades
top_stories.summary: A Democratic sweep of Congress unsettled global markets, with Asian tech shares falling, the dollar weakening and Treasuries rallying. Investors are pricing in tougher scrutiny of Trump's agenda across AI and crypto.

top_stories.title: PC makers shift production back to China
top_stories.summary: HP and Asus are moving some PC manufacturing from Thailand and Vietnam back to China, with Dell reportedly considering it too. Rising memory and processor costs, and IDC's 20.1% fall in Q3 PC shipments, are driving the shift.

top_stories.title: Drax plans AI datacentre at UK's biggest power plant
top_stories.summary: Drax has agreed a deal with Brookfield and Radiant for a datacentre at its North Yorkshire site, with potential investment above £20bn and eventual capacity over 1GW. Drax's market value rose almost 9%.

top_stories.title: Google makes AI opt-in for school students
top_stories.summary: Gemini and other AI features will be off by default for K-12 student accounts, and schools that keep AI disabled will lose access to Google Search. The move reverses an August decision and drew criticism from New York's mayor.

rumour_watch.note: Oracle reportedly dropped a $7bn Tencent AI deal under Trump administration pressure; it rests on a single FT report with no comment from either company, so treat as unconfirmed but plausible given US China-tech policy.
Apple's reported HomeView Ultra with a swivelling robotic display, citing The Information, is credible given the company's smart-home plans, though pricing and 2027-2028 timing are estimates.
Android Authority found code for a YouTube social app called Tamba; strong evidence of a test project, but whether it will launch is unclear.
VNG's reported consideration of a US listing comes from Bloomberg with anonymous sources and no timing; plausible but early.

in_brief.line: AMD's Data Center segment rose 97% to $8.5bn, with analysts suggesting it could become the largest x86 chip vendor.
US tech stocks recovered on Tuesday after the Nasdaq entered correction territory on Monday; Nvidia rose 2.3%.
EU Advocate General says Google's Gemini may infringe press publishers' rights when bypassing paywalls or reusing text.
Democrats flipped Senate seats in several states and took the Texas Senate race, with the White House blaming fuel prices and cost of living.
UK AI minister says a serious cyber breach in public and private sectors is extremely likely, and neither is ready.
Revolut says it cut AI coding inference costs by about 90% by self-hosting Chinese open-weight models.
OpenAI says its GPT-6 Astra model helped design a hardware device in under a week, with a contract manufacturer making prototypes.
Russia added Apple and Microsoft to its register of digital communication providers, requiring local data storage and access on request.

Finance.title: AI trade cracks after US midterms, markets sell off
Finance.notification: Wall Street's AI rally cracks after the midterms, with Nasdaq in correction and Asian chip stocks sliding.
Finance.summary:
The dominant story is a sharp sell-off in AI and tech shares after Democrats won Congress in the US midterms. Investors fear tougher AI regulation and local opposition to data centres could slow the building needed for AI models. The Nasdaq fell 5.5% on Thursday and entered correction territory, and the S&P 500 lost 4.4%. Analysts warn that circular investment among AI firms such as Nvidia, OpenAI and Anthropic could spread losses if one player struggles.

The shock spread across the world. Korea's Kospi plunged, Japan's Nikkei fell 5.5% and Taiwan's TAIEX dropped more than 8%, while European shares fell on Friday. In the UK the FTSE 100 closed 1% lower at 10,673.94, with sterling weaker near $1.3362 as the US jobs report showed payrolls rising by 165,000 and traders priced a likely December Federal Reserve rate rise.

Nvidia faces its own crisis: its board has opened an independent investigation into allegations linked to Chinese intelligence, after CEO Jensen Huang admitted to an affair. Some markets, notably India, have rallied on cheaper crude and hopes of an end to the Iran war, though analysts see this as a relief move rather than a full recovery.

highlights.label: US
highlights.text: Nasdaq entered correction after AI and chip stocks slid on data-centre and regulation fears. Nvidia faces a board probe over CEO Jensen Huang's alleged spy ties.

highlights.label: US
highlights.text: Tesla fell 10.1% and SpaceX 5% after the midterms, while defence stocks dropped on hopes of an end to the Iran war.

highlights.label: UK
highlights.text: FTSE 100 fell 1% to 10,673.94 as AI worries hit tech, IAG's operating profit dropped 16%, and Man Group slumped 7.7%.

highlights.label: Europe
highlights.text: France's borrowing costs are at their widest spread over German bonds since the financial crisis, with interest bills projected above €79bn in 2026.

highlights.label: Asia
highlights.text: Kospi closed down 5.28% and is more than 42% below its June peak, while India's Nifty and Sensex rose nearly 9% in a week.

highlights.label: Asia
highlights.text: The Philippine economy grew just 2.1% in Q3 and inflation hit 7.8%, prompting further central bank rate rises.

points.text: STOXX 600 fell 1.6% early on Friday, wiping out its weekly gains, while Japan's Nikkei fell 5.5%.
Nvidia's board opened an independent probe into whether Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort.
China extended its pause on an extra 24% tariff on US goods to January and will keep its 10% rate.
IAG's chief executive warned that planned green charges falling on UK carriers will kill Europe's aviation industry.
Pop Mart's Labubu sales fell by as much as 50% year on year, and its shares are down more than half from peak.
Five EU leaders urged deeper UK-EU ties ahead of a 20 November Brussels summit attended by Andy Burnham.

World.title: US turns hard right after midterm rout
World.notification: Trump names Stephen Miller chief of staff after midterm losses, as Democrats prepare to take Congress in January.
World.summary:
The US political story dominates the day. Republicans lost heavily in the midterms, with Democrats winning the House and a Senate majority, and President Trump has responded by naming hardline immigration adviser Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff from Monday. Susie Wiles moves to the political operation. Trump has also floated Dana White for press secretary, though he later said he was "only kidding". Markets were rattled, with Trump blaming the result for a one-day loss of about $3 trillion in stock value.

Abroad, the most serious story is the Krakow market-square shooting in Poland, where six people were killed and a British national is among the dead. Authorities describe the gunman as holding far-right and ultranationalist views. In Paraguay, former president Santiago Peña has been impeached and placed under house arrest after the collapse of Ueno Bank, which has frozen accounts for around 60 per cent of adults. In Israel, President Herzog has asked Gadi Eisenkot to try to form a government, a possible end to Netanyahu's long tenure.

In the UK, Andy Burnham's government faces a row over its Remembrance Sunday Erasmus+ pitch and closer EU ties, while Asia's stories include Delhi's smog, China's tariff extensions and Middle East tensions after Houthi strikes on Riyadh.

highlights.label: US
highlights.text: Stephen Miller takes over as White House chief of staff from Monday, after Republicans lost Congress. Democrats vowed investigations into his conduct.

highlights.label: US
highlights.text: Trump said he was 'only kidding' about offering UFC boss Dana White the press secretary job, though White still plans a Monday White House meeting.

highlights.label: UK
highlights.text: Labour's Erasmus+ pitch in a Remembrance Sunday statement has drawn Conservative anger and veterans' criticism, and calls for an apology.

highlights.label: UK
highlights.text: At least a dozen Labour MPs have raised concerns over the draft Conversion Practices Bill, with a parliamentary committee now scrutinising it.

highlights.label: Europe
highlights.text: Poland's Tusk called the Krakow attack terrorism and declared national mourning, with UK, US and EU leaders condemning it.

highlights.label: Europe
highlights.text: France's borrowing spread over German bunds is near its highest since the financial crisis, at about 1.6 points, raising market concern.

points.text: Paraguay's Congress impeached Peña 44-1 in the Senate; he was placed under house arrest, and the vice-president was sworn in.
Eisenkot has 67 endorsements from 120 Knesset members but relies on Arab-led parties he has ruled out; Netanyahu has 46.
Burnham says closer EU food and farming ties could cut living costs; deals are due to be signed in Brussels on 20 November.
Trump says US will end military aid to Israel by end-2026, a 10-year deal worth $3.8bn a year; Israel faces about $10bn in orders.
Aramco Tower in Riyadh was hit in a Houthi air attack, lifting oil prices as Saudi air defences intercepted missiles.
Iran says mediators have stopped travelling since the midterms; the US Task Force Iron Gate extends its blockade to land routes.

Tech.title: Nvidia's Huang faces congressional scrutiny over spy probe
Tech.notification: Nvidia's Jensen Huang is called to Congress as a probe into a reported Chinese spy link deepens.
Tech.summary:
The dominant tech story is the reported Chinese spy probe involving Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang. Three Republican House committee chairs have arranged a closed-door meeting with him over national security concerns, after New York Times reporting that Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore data centre firm Megaspeed, may be a Chinese asset. Huang has apologised to staff for an affair, and Nvidia's board has opened an independent investigation, saying it sees no sign that secrets or national security were compromised. No one has been charged, and the Chinese government and embassy deny the allegations.

The wider context is a sharp tech sell-off. Anthropic is reportedly pressing ahead with an IPO before Thanksgiving at a lower valuation, while OpenAI has reportedly trimmed its funding target. Investors are reacting to rising borrowing costs, heavy AI spending and fears that newly elected Democrats could slow data centre construction. Those political fears run through a wider backlash: local data centre bans, protests in Europe and a report that most public comments at local meetings oppose new facilities.

Supply strains are also visible. Memory shortages are pushing up prices of graphics cards, consoles and devices such as the Raspberry Pi 5, while Samsung and SK hynix are sitting on huge cash piles and planning record investment. Export controls remain under scrutiny after reports that Nvidia H200 chips were approved for buyers with questionable links.

highlights.label: Anthropic IPO
highlights.text: Anthropic reportedly wants to raise $80-100bn at a $1.25-1.75tn valuation, accepting less than backers hoped, amid the tech selloff.

highlights.label: Tesla
highlights.text: Musk says Cybertruck production at Texas Gigafactory will wind down around mid-2027 to make room for Cybercab and Optimus.

highlights.label: Samsung and SK hynix
highlights.text: The two chipmakers hold 329.3tn won in cash, with Samsung planning record capex of 84.4tn won.

highlights.label: Data centre backlash
highlights.text: A new analysis of 10,202 public comments found about 90% opposed data centre developments at local meetings.

highlights.label: Asia rebound
highlights.text: Asian stocks bounced after last week's AI-led rout, which had pushed several regional indices into bear territory.

highlights.label: AI safety
highlights.text: METR says Anthropic may have crossed its own AI acceleration warning threshold in July, though it still rates catastrophic risk as low.

points.text: Analyst Jeffrey Sonnenfeld puts the odds of Huang keeping his job at about 50-50; Huang remains CEO for now.
Reports say Nvidia approached Apollo about converting Brightspeed telecom sites into small AI data centres after a 9% share drop.
A lawsuit against OpenAI alleges ChatGPT helped a man's wife plan a poisoning, the tenth such homicide-linked case reported.
Will Lawrence, who campaigned against data centres, won a Michigan House seat and plans to push for a federal moratorium.
Apple plans to bring Alibaba's Qwen into Apple Intelligence in China from December, while Samsung uses Baidu's Ernie.
The US trial of Huawei in Brooklyn is in its defence phase, with prosecutors alleging theft of technology and sanctions breaches.

Fashion.title: Martine Rose takes the Balenciaga creative director chair
Fashion.notification: Martine Rose is named Balenciaga's creative director, the first woman to lead the Kering house in its 109-year history.
Fashion.summary:
Balenciaga has named British designer Martine Rose as creative director, succeeding Pierpaolo Piccioli, whose departure was announced after 18 months. She becomes the first woman to lead the Kering-owned house in its 109-year history and will oversee both the men's and women's lines. Rose previously worked on Balenciaga menswear under Demna for three years and runs her own London label, which has not staged a show since June 2025.

The appointment is part of a wider portfolio overhaul at Kering under chief executive Luca de Meo, and it draws strong early praise, with coverage highlighting her streetwear-meets-high-fashion appeal and high-profile fans such as Rihanna and Kendrick Lamar. Investors are watching Kering's shares, while the change in creative leadership signals how the group intends to reposition one of its most closely watched labels.

Elsewhere, the calendar is busy. Max Mara Fashion Group launched a new everyday womenswear label, M-M For Mondays and More, its eleventh brand, while Ferrari Style opened its first New York flagship in SoHo. The Met Gala has also unveiled its 2027 exhibition theme, extraORDINARY, after a planned Galliano retrospective was cancelled.

highlights.label: Balenciaga

highlights.label: Yeezy
highlights.text: Ye returns with a Los Angeles runway show, his first formal show since 2022 and without Adidas; GQ finds it restrained.
